entries.topic: 1923–1925: Lausanne, the Mandate in force, and Palestinian citizenship

claims.text: The peace treaty between the Allies and Turkey was signed at Lausanne on 24 July 1923.
The Treaty of Lausanne entered into force on 6 August 1924.

The Republic of Turkey renounced its rights over the former Arab provinces in the Treaty of Lausanne; Professor John Quigley stresses that the renunciation was not made in favour of Britain or the Allies.
The League Council had approved the Palestine and Syria mandates on 24 July 1922 on condition that they take effect once France and Italy reached a final agreement over Syria.

Minutes of the League Council meeting of 29 September 1923, as reproduced by the UN, record that the mandates for Syria and Palestine "had thereby automatically and simultaneously entered into force"; Sir Rennell Rodd said the question was "finally settled".

Quigley argues the Council minutes used future-tense wording and took no resolution, and that Secretary-General Eric Drummond's Circular Letter 101 recast this in the past tense; on his reading the 29 September 1923 date has no legal force and Britain held Palestine without title.
The Palestinian Citizenship Order was issued on 24 July 1925 and took effect on 1 August 1925, applying to Ottoman subjects habitually resident in Palestine on that date.

According to Abu Alia and Khalil, the Government of Palestine reportedly accepted about 100 of some 9,000 naturalization applications under an "absolute discretion" clause in one period, and by 1946 about 130,000 foreigners had acquired Palestinian citizenship by naturalization, 99 percent of them Jews.

Historian Lauren Banko describes the 1925 Order as the first Mandate legislation to treat the Arab population as citizens rather than "ex-enemy Ottoman subjects", and notes it denied citizenship to Arabs who had emigrated abroad.

Banko argues the Order treated Jewish citizenship and immigrant naturalization in sharp contrast to Arab citizenship, and that Palestinian Arabs answered it by invoking Ottoman-era principles of descent and birthplace.

disputes.question: When, and whether lawfully, did the Mandate enter into force?

positions.view: 29 September 1923: the League Council minutes record the Palestine and Syria mandates entering into force automatically and simultaneously; Britain, the League Secretariat and the UN in 1947 treated this as the date.

No valid entry into force: Quigley argues the Council set no date and took no resolution, that the past-tense formula was Drummond's, and that Lausanne (in force only on 6 August 1924) gave Britain no title.

disputes.question: Date the League approved the Mandate text

positions.view: 24 July 1922 (UN document).
12 August 1922 (footnote in Abu Alia and Khalil).

entries.topic: Immigration 1923–1936: the Fourth and Fifth Aliyot and the two official series

claims.text: The same 1939 memorandum cites a Consul General report of 10 January 1939 that the Jewish population had risen sixfold since 1920, almost entirely through immigration, while the Arab population had risen about 57 percent, almost entirely through natural increase.

A State Department memorandum of 6 November 1936 (Paul Alling) cites Palestine Government statistics that 61,854 Jews entered in 1935, of whom 14,653 came under the labour schedule and 13,076 were their dependants; Alling estimates the remaining 44,000 entered in other categories such as capital holders, professionals and skilled artisans.
The Alling memorandum lists labour-schedule allotments of 5,500 for April–September 1933 rising to 8,000 for April–September 1935, then 3,250 for October 1935–March 1936.

The Jewish Virtual Library states that the Fourth Aliyah (1924–1929) brought 82,000 Jews to Palestine, of whom 23,000 left, that most were middle class with modest capital, and that the Yishuv suffered an economic crisis in 1926–1928.

The JVL attributes the Fourth Aliyah to the economic crisis and anti-Jewish policies in Poland and to stiff US immigration quotas; the US Immigration Act of 1924 limited annual immigration from each country to 2 percent of its residents in the 1890 census.

The Shaw Commission (1930) criticised "excessive" immigration in 1925–26 and quoted Sir John Campbell that the 1927–28 crisis came from immigrants arriving "in excess of the economic absorbing power of the country".
The JVL states that nearly 250,000 Jews arrived during the Fifth Aliyah by 1940 (20,000 later left), that 174,000 settled in 1933–1936 alone, and that the Yishuv reached 450,000 by 1940.
Tel Aviv had about 15,000 people in 1922, 34,000 in 1925, 45,564 in 1931 and 120,000 in 1935; it received municipal status on 12 May 1934.

disputes.question: How many Jewish immigrants arrived each year?

positions.view: Recorded immigration as compiled by the US State Department from British returns (e.g. 30,327 in 1933, 61,854 in 1935).

Higher series printed by the JVL from Porath (e.g. 37,337 in 1933, 66,472 in 1935); the sources do not explain the difference, which may reflect how unrecorded or later-registered arrivals were counted.

entries.topic: 1925: the Hebrew University and Brit Shalom

claims.text: Twelve foundation stones of the Hebrew University were laid on Mount Scopus on 24 July 1918; Einstein gave its first lecture in 1923.

The university was opened on 1 April 1925 by Arthur Balfour, with Chaim Weizmann presiding as chairman of the board; Judah Magnes was its chancellor, later president, and the first degrees were awarded in 1931.
A Detroit Jewish Chronicle report of 10 April 1925 described "excitement" among Jerusalem Arabs at a rumour that Balfour would visit the Omar Mosque and said no incidents occurred.

Brit Shalom (Berit Shalom) was founded in Jerusalem in 1925 on the initiative of Arthur Ruppin, prompted by a lecture by Prof. Joseph Horowitz at the university's opening; it sought a binational arrangement with Jews and Arabs sharing administration equally regardless of numbers.

Its early members included Ruppin, Jacob Thon, Joseph Lurie, Yitzhak Epstein, Haim Margolis-Kalvaryski and Rabbi Binyamin; after 1929 Central European intellectuals influenced by Martin Buber predominated, among them Hugo Bergmann, Hans Kohn, Gershom Scholem, Ernst Simon and Robert Weltsch.
Brit Shalom never had more than 200 members; Ruppin chaired it until 1929; its monthly She'ifoteinu appeared 1930–33; most Zionist parties attacked it, and by 1933 it had virtually ceased to exist.
Judah Magnes advocated binationalism in this period but, according to the Encyclopaedia Judaica text on the JVL, was never a member of Brit Shalom, though his name was often linked to it.

disputes.question: Was Judah Magnes a founder of Brit Shalom?

positions.view: Never a member, though associated with its views (Encyclopaedia Judaica via JVL).

Elsewhere in the simulation (scene s00b3) Buber and Magnes are called "both founders of Brit Shalom (1925)"; the writer should state the conflict. (Position held in the simulation scene, with that scene's own citations; no new source.)

entries.topic: The Western Wall / al-Buraq dispute and the August 1929 violence, 1928–1930

claims.text: In September 1928, on Yom Kippur, Jewish worshippers set up a portable screen at the Western Wall to separate men and women; its removal opened the dispute.

On 15 August 1929 a few hundred Jewish youths, Betar members among them, marched to the Wall and raised a flag; on 16 August a Muslim demonstration went to the Wall, beat Jews there and burned prayer notes.
The Shaw Commission found the outbreak began in Jerusalem on 23 August 1929 as an attack by Arabs on Jews, that it "was not premeditated", and that it was not a revolt against British authority.
In Hebron on 24 August 1929 the killing began at about 9 a.m.; eight American students of the Slobodka Yeshiva were among the dead.
The Zionist Archives list 435 Hebron Jews who found refuge in 28 Arab homes, according to Human Rights Watch; Norman Bentwich wrote that many Jews were saved by Arab neighbours.
In Safed on 29 August 1929 between 18 and 20 Jews were killed and about 80 wounded; some 200 Jewish homes were burned.

The week's dead totalled 133 Jews and 116 Arabs; most Arab deaths were caused by British police and military fire during suppression. Only about 150 British police and 1,500 local police served the whole country.

Britain's 1929 report to the League recorded collective punishments on towns and villages that took part in attacks on Jews at Hebron, Safad, Motza, Artuf and Beer Tuvia, with fines totalling £P17,840.
By the end of December 1929, 791 Arabs and 66 Jews had been tried summarily; 17 Arabs and 1 Jew had received capital sentences, and 7 death sentences had been confirmed on appeal.
On 17 June 1930 three Arab men were hanged in Acre for their part in the riots, and 25 other death sentences, two of them on Jews, were commuted; Palestinians remember the day as "Red Tuesday".

The Shaw Commission found no evidence that the Mufti, Hajj Amin al-Husseini, incited the outbreak but held that he "must accept a share in the responsibility"; it found premeditation not proved against the Arab Executive.

Shaw named the fundamental cause as Arab hostility rooted in disappointed political aspirations and fear for their economic future; immediate causes included the Wall incidents of September 1928–16 August 1929, the 15 August Jewish demonstration, inflammatory press and the enlargement of the Jewish Agency.

A League commission of three non-British members (Eliel Löfgren of Sweden, Charles Barde of Geneva, J. van Kempen of the Netherlands) sat in Jerusalem from 19 June to 19 July 1930 and reported in December 1930.

The 1930 commission found that the Wall and the pavement in front of it are Muslim property, that the Wall is "sacred to both Parties", and that Jews have free access for devotions but may bring only appurtenances permitted under the Turkish regime, with screens separating men and women barred.

disputes.question: How many Jews died in the August 1929 violence?

positions.view: 133 Jews and 116 Arabs (EBSCO reference; JVL).
113 Jews and 116 Arabs, with Palestinian casualties likely under-reported by the Mandate (Jerusalem Story lexicon).
Palestinian account: a provocation by Betar-led demonstrators who raised the Zionist flag at a site under Muslim authority, against fear of a takeover of the holy places.
Jewish account: a Muslim campaign led by the Mufti over the Wall and incitement, culminating in massacres of unarmed communities.
Shaw Commission: no premeditation; a share of responsibility on the Mufti; the 15 August demonstration the most significant immediate cause.
67 Jews killed (HRW gives the date as 23 August).
One yeshiva student killed on 23 August and 64 killed at the Heichal residence on 24 August (EBSCO).

entries.topic: Land and labour in the official inquiries of 1930

claims.text: Sir John Hope Simpson's Report on Immigration, Land Settlement and Development (Cmd. 3686) carries a covering letter dated 22 August 1930 and was published in October 1930.

Hope Simpson adopted the Director of Surveys' estimate of 8,044,000 metric dunams of cultivable land, including 1,500,000 in the Beersheba region, and found that the cultivable share of the hills was only 40 per cent, not 66.6 per cent as assumed.
He put Jewish-held land in June 1930 at about 1,250,000 (Turkish) dunams and, after deducting about 900,000 metric dunams of Jewish holdings, left 5,644,000 metric dunams for non-Jewish cultivators.
In 104 surveyed villages 6,940 of 23,573 families, 29.4 per cent, held no land.

His own enquiry found that of 688 Arab families displaced by land sales only 379 were cultivating land again and 309 had joined the landless; he estimated land available for new settlement at "100,000 dunams at the outside".

Hope Simpson quoted the Keren Kayemeth (Jewish National Fund) draft lease requiring the lessee to cultivate "only with Jewish labour", on penalty of ten Palestinian pounds per breach and repossession after three breaches.
He noted that the Jewish Agency's 1920 constitution committed it to colonisation "based on Jewish labour", and that less than one in three post-1921 immigrants settled on the land.

The Shaw Commission found that the 1920 and 1921 Land Transfer Ordinances had failed, that the 1929 Protection of Cultivators Ordinance did not stop evictions, and that evictions were creating a landless class, "a potential danger to the country".
Shaw also called the allocation of Labour Schedule certificates by political creed indefensible and found that Jewish immigration within absorptive capacity had brought material benefits.
A 1931 Jewish Agency memorandum, "The Statistical Bases of Sir John Hope Simpson's Report", was published to contest the report's figures.

disputes.question: Was there room for further Jewish agricultural settlement in 1930?

positions.view: Hope Simpson: without development there was no margin; at most 100,000 dunams were available and a landless class was forming.
The Jewish Agency contested the statistical basis of the report in a 1931 memorandum.

entries.topic: What the MacDonald letter of 13 February 1931 said

claims.text: The letter presented itself as the "authoritative interpretation" of the October 1930 White Paper and stated that the government did not contemplate "any stoppage or prohibition of Jewish immigration".
It tied limits on immigration to the absorptive principle, described as "purely economic considerations".

It said the 1930 policy did not bar further Jewish land purchase and referred only to "temporary control of land disposition and transfers"; the duty to settle landless Arabs applied to those displaced by land passing into Jewish hands.
It described the Mandate as "an undertaking to the Jewish people and not only to the Jewish population of Palestine", a double undertaking to which equal weight was to be given.

It accepted the Jewish Agency's right to affirm preferential employment of Jewish labour, but said the Mandatory must take account of any resulting displacement of Arab labour or rise in unemployment.

On 30 June 1936, 137 Arab senior government officials told the High Commissioner the Arabs had lost faith in official pledges, citing the 1931 letter issued as an interpretation of the 1930 White Paper, and recommended stopping immigration.

entries.topic: Palestinian politics, 1928–1935: congresses, women, the Islamic Congress, parties

claims.text: Raghib al-Nashashibi's opposition bloc attended the Seventh Palestinian Arab Congress in June 1928 and he joined the Arab Executive that emerged from it.
Nashashibi, appointed mayor of Jerusalem in 1920, was re-elected in 1927 and served until 1934, when Hussein Fakhri al-Khalidi was elected.

The first Palestine Arab Women's Congress met in Jerusalem on 26 October 1929 with about 300 delegates, led by Salma al-Husseini and organised by Wahida al-Khalidi and Amina al-Husseini; it called for repeal of the Balfour Declaration and an end to Jewish immigration and elected a 14-member executive.
Jamal al-Husseini sat on the Arab Executive delegation that negotiated in London in April and May 1930; Nashashibi travelled with it in March 1930.

The General Islamic Congress opened in Jerusalem on 7 December 1931 with 130 delegates from 22 countries, Hajj Amin al-Husseini among its main organisers; it resolved to defend the holy places, boycott Zionist goods, found an Islamic university in Jerusalem and form a company to buy Palestinian land.

High Commissioner Wauchope questioned the Mufti over the delegates' political speeches; Britain deported Abd al-Rahman Azzam and refused entry to the former caliph Abdulmecid II; the university project stalled for lack of funds in 1935.
In December 1931 Nashashibi held a rival conference in Jerusalem to counter the Mufti's congress.

The Istiqlal (Independence) Party was officially announced in August 1932 by eleven founders including Rashid al-Haj Ibrahim, Awni Abd al-Hadi and Muhammad Izzat Darwaza; it called for full Arab independence and unity and named British imperialism as the main enemy.
Istiqlal never built a large membership; its influence peaked among young educated Palestinians in early 1933 and then fell, partly through Husseini hostility and lack of funds.

The Murison Commission found that the October 1933 disturbances (Jerusalem 13 October; Jaffa, Haifa and Nablus 27–28 October; Jerusalem again 28–29 October) followed an Arab Executive call for protest demonstrations and were "aimed against the Government and not against the Jews".

Murison counted 1 policeman and 26 members of the public killed and 56 police and 187 public injured; all public deaths were by gunfire, 15 of them at Jaffa, where police fired 102 rifle and 43 revolver rounds. The commission, reporting on 4 January 1934, found the police had acted with restraint.

Nashashibi founded the National Defense Party in early December 1934, rejecting the Balfour Declaration, Jewish immigration and land sales and calling for parliamentary government; he was close to Emir Abdullah.
The Palestine Arab Party was officially established on 27 March 1935, with Jamal al-Husseini, close to the Mufti, unanimously chosen as leader.
By late 1935 the five Arab parties had formed a united front, which a US consul described as a response to a "national emergency".

disputes.question: Was Britain's use of force in October 1933 justified?

positions.view: Murison Commission: police acted "with restraint and forbearance" and no officer departed from regulations.
The demonstrations were political protest against government policy, and all 26 civilian dead were killed by police gunfire; Musa Kazim al-Husseini was injured at Jaffa (see pp_s01).

claims.text: Al-Qassam was born in 1882 in Jabla, south of Latakia, studied at al-Azhar in Cairo, joined the 1919–20 revolt against the French on the Syrian coast and was sentenced to death by the French.
He moved to Haifa in late 1920 (December 1920 in another account), taught at the Burj school and became imam and preacher at the Istiqlal Mosque.
In July 1928 he was elected president of the Haifa branch of the Young Men's Muslim Association, and in 1930 he was appointed a ma'dhun by the Haifa Shari'a court.

Accounts of his clandestine organisation describe cells of no more than five, with units for preaching, intelligence and military training, and guerrilla attacks on Jewish settlements from 1931 that soon paused after leaks to the British.
In autumn 1935 Qassam wrote to Rashid al-Haj Ibrahim of his plan to take to the hills; according to Al Majalla, the Mufti declined to back a revolt, saying the time was not right.
On 12 November 1935 he declared jihad in Haifa and left for the forests of Ya'bad near Jenin with about eleven companions.

On 20 November 1935 he was killed in a six-hour fight with a larger British police force near Ya'bad; a US consul reported that his bands caused one British constable's death, and that four of his men died and five were captured.
Haifa declared a general strike on 21 November 1935 and held its largest funeral procession; he was buried at Balad al-Shaykh.
In 1991 Hamas named its military wing the Qassam Brigades after him.

disputes.question: How large was his following, and how many died with him?

positions.view: Al Majalla, from British archives: 50–200 fighters; it calls a claim of 800 "grossly exaggerated"; it says he died with two colleagues.
Palquest: Qassam and four of his men were killed; the US consul likewise reports four of his men killed and five captured.
Palestinian accounts present him as a leader of resistance to British occupation whose death helped ignite the 1936–39 revolt.
His group's attacks targeted Jewish settlers as well as the British; he called for confronting Jewish settlers "as enemies and not as immigrants or guests".

claims.text: The Union of Zionists-Revisionists held its founding conference in Paris in 1925; its first president was Vladimir Tiomkin, and it had four delegates at the Fourteenth Zionist Congress that year.

In 1931 the Revisionists won 17 percent of the vote for the Yishuv's elected assembly (Asefat ha-Nivharim), becoming its second-largest party, and sent 52 delegates to the Seventeenth Zionist Congress in Basel, where they proposed a resolution for a Jewish state on both sides of the Jordan.

In 1933 at Katowice Jabotinsky suspended the party executive; a membership plebiscite backed him, and opponents led by Meir Grossman seceded to form the Jewish State Party, which had seven delegates to the Revisionists' 46 at the Eighteenth Congress.
In 1934 more than 600,000 Jews in 24 countries signed a Revisionist petition addressed to the British king and Parliament.

In 1935 the Zionist General Council adopted a "discipline clause" barring independent political action; a Revisionist plebiscite chose secession, and the New Zionist Organization's constituent assembly met in Vienna in September 1935, said to have been "elected by 713,000 voters", with Jabotinsky as president.

disputes.question: What does the "600,000" figure for 1934 count?

positions.view: Encyclopaedia Judaica (via encyclopedia.com): signatures on a 1934 petition in 24 countries.

entries.topic: The Arlosoroff murder and the Labor–Revisionist conflict, 1933–1935

claims.text: Chaim Arlosoroff, head of the Jewish Agency's political department, was shot on the Tel Aviv beach on the night of 16 June 1933 while walking with his wife Sima, and died early on 17 June.
He had returned from Germany about two days earlier; the Center for Israel Education links the trip to the Haavara transfer agreement, which was formally signed on 25 August 1933.
Three Revisionists were charged: Abba Ahimeir with plotting the killing, and Avraham Stavsky and Zvi Rosenblatt as the gunmen; Sima Arlosoroff identified Stavsky and Rosenblatt.
Only Stavsky was convicted, and he was cleared on appeal in 1934 for lack of corroborating evidence; no one else was ever charged.

Jabotinsky campaigned for more than a year for the accused, whom he believed innocent; at the Eighteenth Zionist Congress in Prague (21 August–3 September 1933) the Revisionists were accused of the murder.

A three-member commission chaired by former Supreme Court Justice David Bechor, appointed by Menachem Begin's government in March 1982, reported in June 1985: it cleared Ahimeir, Stavsky and Rosenblatt, could not determine who killed Arlosoroff or whether it was a political act, and cleared the Labor movement of the Revisionist charge of a "blood libel".
In 1934 Ben-Gurion and Jabotinsky signed three agreements in London; the labour agreement was rejected in a Histadrut referendum.

The Histadrut plebiscite was held on 25 March 1935; early returns showed about 12,000 against and 9,000 for, with Tel Aviv 3,983 against to 3,296 for and Haifa 3,785 against to 1,555 for. Haaretz called the result "a grave mishap for the entire Zionist movement".

positions.view: Labor accusation in 1933: Revisionist extremists (the three accused).
The accused were acquitted in 1934 and cleared by the 1985 Bechor commission, which could not identify the killers.

entries.topic: The Haganah after 1929, the 1931 split, and the 1935 arms shipment

claims.text: The Histadrut took responsibility for defence at its founding in December 1920 and the Haganah was placed under its direct control; through the 1920s it had only "a few hundred" volunteer members.
Senior commanders drew up a "Constitution of the Haganah" in 1924; in 1926 former Ha-Shomer members formed a separate underground within the Gedud ha-Avodah.

In August 1929 Haganah volunteers helped defend the Jewish communities of Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa; massacres occurred where it was absent or weak (Hebron, Safed, Motza), which drove a shift toward wider organisation and public control.

In 1931 a six-member national command was formed with parity between three Histadrut members (Eliyahu Golomb, Dov Hos, Meir Rutberg) and three non-labour members; the commander who opposed public control was removed.
A group led by Avraham Tehomi, Jerusalem district commander from 1929 to 1931, seceded and with Revisionist groups formed the Irgun Zvai Leumi; Tehomi returned to the Haganah in 1937.
In 1931–35 the Haganah had urban branches in Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa with memberships "in the hundreds", annual officers' courses, and workshops producing hand grenades.
In 1935 rifles and ammunition were shipped from Belgium hidden in barrels of cement; British authorities seized 537 barrels at Jaffa port, which caused significant unrest among Palestinian Arabs.

One account gives the contents as 25 Lewis machine guns, 800 rifles and 400,000 rounds found in 359 of the drums, consigned to a merchant in Tel Aviv who was never identified, and dates a protest general strike to 26 October 1935.

entries.topic: The Mandate economy, 1922–1936: the Jewish Agency's case and the oil pipeline

claims.text: David Horowitz of the Jewish Agency's Economics Department prepared "Economic and Social Transformation of Palestine" (1937) for the Agency's case before the Peel Commission; it is an advocacy document.

Horowitz stated that "LP 80,000,000 have been invested by Jews in economic enterprise" over sixteen years, with annual Jewish building investment rising from LP 900,000 in 1924 to LP 7,000,000 in 1935.
He gave the Jewish population as 84,000 (13 percent) in 1922 and 375,000 (28 percent) in 1935, and the non-Jewish population as 565,000 in 1922 and 975,000 in 1935.
He gave government revenue as LP 2,371,000 in 1922–23 and LP 5,452,000 in 1934–35, and expenditure rising from LP 1,900,000 to LP 3,200,000.

He gave citrus exports rising from £200,000 in 1921 to £2,700,000 in 1934 and the citrus area from 30,000 dunams (1922) to 260,000 (1935); industrial output from under LP 1,000,000 in 1921 to over LP 8,000,000 in 1935.

Horowitz argued that Arabs gained directly from Jewish contributions to revenue, from land prices up 400–500 percent, and from falling death rates in districts of Jewish immigration; he cited daily wages of 10–15 piastres in Palestine against 2–3 in Iraq and Egypt.

The Iraq Petroleum Company pipeline split at Haditha into branches to Tripoli and Haifa; it was built 1932–1934, first oil reached Haifa on 16 October 1934, and the line had a capacity of four million tons a year.

Transit agreements with Palestine, Transjordan, Lebanon and Syria were signed between 5 January and 25 March 1931; official opening ceremonies were held in January 1935; Iraq stopped sending oil to Haifa in 1948.

disputes.question: Did Arabs benefit from Jewish investment?

positions.view: Jewish Agency (Horowitz 1937): revenue, wages, land prices and health gains flowed to Arabs.
Hope Simpson (1930): Jewish National Fund leases required Jewish labour only, a landless Arab class was forming, and displaced families were not resettled (see hope_simpson_land_1930).

disputes.question: Jewish share of the population in 1922

claims.text: On 23 December 1935 High Commissioner Sir Arthur Wauchope put a proposed legislative council of 14 Arabs, 7 Jews and 7 Britons to Jewish leaders, saying the government was "determined to establish the assembly".

As reported, the basis of representation was fixed for five years, one of the elected Arabs was to be a Bedouin, the High Commissioner could nominate members for a boycotting community, and the council could not deal with the labour immigration schedule.

Weizmann rejected the plan as contrary to the Mandate, citing the Lucerne Congress resolution that it would fix the Jews as a minority; Yitzhak Ben-Zvi for the Vaad Leumi and A. L. Maleh for the Sephardi community concurred; Rabbi Moshe Blau of Agudath Israel said the time was "not yet ripe".
Arab leaders withheld their reply and objected to women voting; the Mufti was reported still opposed.

On 24 March 1936 Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin announced a Commons debate on the council; Colonial Secretary J. H. Thomas said final action would wait for it; JTA reported Jewish organisations "unitedly opposed" and some Arab groups accepting.
A US consul reported in April 1936 that the council proposals had broken the united front of the five Arab parties, and that "all thought of united Arab action" on the council was abandoned.
On 5 May 1936 the Mufti and other Arab leaders declined to attend a London conference on the proposal, according to the Center for Israel Education.

entries.topic: Jews of the Arab world, 1929–1936: Iraq after independence, and Constantine

claims.text: Under the British Mandate in Iraq Jews held government posts and could teach Hebrew, and several Zionist organisations were permitted until 1929.
After independence in 1932 prominent Jews helped build the Iraqi civil service and several sat in the first independent parliament.

According to Sephardi Voices UK, from 1934 Iraqi Jews had to pay a £50 deposit to travel abroad; in 1935 Hebrew teaching was barred and state secondary schools set quotas on Jewish pupils; in 1936 Jews were dismissed from the civil service.
During Rashid Ali al-Gaylani's first premiership (1933), the German chargé d'affaires Fritz Grobba was allowed to publish Mein Kampf in Iraqi newspapers, according to the same source.
In Constantine, French Algeria, in August 1934, 25 Jews and 3 Muslims were killed over a few days of violence.

Historian Joshua Cole (Lethal Provocation, 2019) argues the French colonial state had an interest in "provoking and nurturing" Jewish–Muslim tension to resist extending citizenship rights to Algerian Muslims, and identifies Mohamed El Maadi, a veteran with extreme-right ties, as a key participant.
